worksheet.title: Sort by Shape
worksheet.subtitle: Putting the same things together
worksheet.learning_goal: I can put the shapes that are the same together.

parts.title: Bit's shapes got mixed up
parts.text: Bit dropped a pile of shapes. Help Bit put the same shapes together. Making groups of the same thing is called SORTING.

parts.title: Bit's pile
parts.note: Look: circles, triangles, and squares are all mixed together.

parts.title: Watch Bit sort one group
parts.note: Bit put both circles ● in one group. Now you try the rest.

parts.title: Triangle group  ▲
parts.prompt: Draw all the triangles from the pile in this group.

parts.title: Square group  ■
parts.prompt: Draw all the squares from the pile in this group.

parts.title: You try
parts.prompt: Here is a new little pile: ■ ● ■. Draw only the squares in the boxes.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Putting the same things together is called sorting. Computers sort too — it helps them find things fast!

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children sort a mixed pile of shapes into groups, one kind per group. Sorting into groups is a first thinking-skill behind coding — it is how computers organize information to find it again. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil or crayon. You read each prompt aloud; the child answers by drawing. Optional: real shape blocks or cut-outs to sort by hand first.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Point to Bit's pile: "these are all mixed up." Show the circle group — both circles together.
2. Do one together. Find each triangle in the pile and draw it in the triangle group box.
3. Let them try. Children do the square group, then Exercise 3 on their own.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Pile (circle, triangle, square, circle, triangle, square): circle group = 2, triangle group = 2, square group = 2.
Exercise 1 — 2 triangles. Exercise 2 — 2 squares. Exercise 3 (square, circle, square) — 2 squares (the circle is left out).

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: copying the whole pile into one group. Remind them each group holds only one kind.
Make it easier: sort real objects by hand before drawing.
Make it harder: sort the same pile a different way (by size), or add a star group.
Make it active: place shape cards on the floor and have children walk each one to its group.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children use computational-thinking skills (sorting and classifying by attribute) to make sense of their world.
In plain terms: putting things into groups by one feature (here, shape) — a first sorting skill.
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child answers by drawing or circling.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child puts every shape in the matching group, and no group holds a different shape.
